passage:
Friday night

Third time this month the leader has asked for money "to keep the struggle alive". This time it's twice what we gave before. At the meeting Wasim asked where the last collection went, and the leader said, "Doubters are traitors. Only the weak ask that." Everyone went quiet. A few people clapped, and I clapped too, and I hated my hands for it.

I gave because I believe in the cause. I still do. But if it's real, why can't anyone see the accounts? A real movement should be happy to show them.

Tomorrow I'll ask, politely and in writing, how funds are used before I give another rupee. And I'll talk to my cousin, who isn't in the group.

If they call that betrayal, that tells me something too.

Suraj

qa.q: How many times this month has the leader asked for money?
qa.a: It is the third time this month.

qa.q: Why did Suraj hate the clapping hands afterwards?
qa.a: Suraj clapped along to stay with the crowd after doubters were called traitors, and felt ashamed of joining in on something that felt wrong.

qa.q: What is Suraj planning, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Suraj will ask in writing how funds are used and talk to a cousin outside the group; a real movement welcomes transparency, and an outsider adds perspective.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt after asking where the money went?
qa.a: Wasim was probably embarrassed or isolated, since everyone went quiet after doubters were called traitors, though the question itself was fair.

grounding: A leader keeps asking Suraj for money and calls doubters traitors, so Suraj plans to ask how funds are used and treats forced unity as a warning sign.

passage:
The housing collective met every Thursday in a Lisbon café basement, and every Thursday Rui, the founder, found a new reason for another contribution: banners, a lawyer's fee, a van. Gabriel had already given two months of his bakery tips.

This time Gabriel raised his hand. "Could we see where the last collection went? Just a simple list."

The room went quiet. Rui smiled without warmth. "People who ask for receipts are working for the landlords. Are you with us or not?"

On the tram home Yuki said, "You asked what half of us were thinking." Gabriel's hands were still trembling. He felt foolish and angry at once.

The next week he and Yuki visited a tenants' union across the river. Their treasurer pinned the accounts to the noticeboard every month.

qa.q: Where did the housing collective meet every Thursday?
qa.a: It met every Thursday in a Lisbon café basement.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling on the tram home?
qa.a: Gabriel felt foolish and angry at once, and his trembling hands show how shaken he was by being called disloyal.

qa.q: What was wise about Gabriel's question, and what did he do next?
qa.a: Asking for a simple list of how money was used is fair in any real movement; he then found a group that shares its accounts openly.

qa.q: How does Yuki see the moment Gabriel spoke up?
qa.a: Yuki sees it as brave, because many members shared the same doubt but were afraid to be called traitors.

grounding: The scene shows a movement leader answering a request for transparency with accusations of betrayal, and the member treating that as a warning sign.

passage:
The hostel mess committee room smelled of old files. Trisha had come to drop off her form for the fee-cut campaign, and Farida, the second-year who led it, pushed a donation box across the table.

"Fifth time this month," Trisha said lightly. "What's this one for?"

"Printing. Posters. Does it matter? Doubters are traitors, Trisha. The warden wants us divided."

Trisha put her pen down. Pooja, beside her, went very still.

Later, on the terrace, Pooja admitted she had borrowed money from her cousin to keep paying. They agreed on a plan: at Friday's general meeting they would ask, politely and together, for a written list of expenses. If Farida refused, they would take their concerns to the student council.

On Friday, three more students stood up and asked the same question.

qa.q: How many times had Trisha been asked to give that month?
qa.a: It was the fifth time that month, as Trisha said.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when Farida called doubters traitors?
qa.a: Pooja felt frightened and trapped, going very still, and later admitted she had borrowed money to keep paying.

qa.q: What small step did Trisha and Pooja choose, and why is it wise?
qa.a: They chose to ask together, politely, for a written list of expenses, because a real campaign can show where money goes.

qa.q: How might Farida see the students who stood up on Friday?
qa.a: Farida may see them as a threat to Farida's control, but to most members they show that asking questions is normal, not betrayal.

grounding: The hostel scene shows students recognising pressure to give money and forced unity as warning signs and asking openly how funds are used.
